The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

Sanofi: predictable earnings on a floor multiple; the share price turns on what management buys to bridge 2031, and what it pays

Sanofi (SAN-FR): investment memo

24 November 2026. Share price EUR 83.79 (20 November 2026). The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, update 2, which includes an assumed EUR 10bn debt-funded acquisition in mid-2027. Probabilities are my judgements. Terms, the limits of the evidence and data clarifications are in the end-notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one paragraph. Sanofi offers 18 months of unusually predictable earnings at a multiple near the floor of its ten-year history, but its share price will be decided by a question those earnings do not answer: can investors see past March 2031, when Dupixent's US composition patent expires? Dupixent, the immunology drug Sanofi shares with Regeneron, is about 43% of 2026 sales and roughly half of operating profit. The model has business EPS (Sanofi's adjusted earnings per share, the figure consensus tracks) of EUR 9.02 in 2026, up 15%, then growth of 6% to 8% a year to EUR 11.08 in 2029. The shares trade on 8.2 times two-year-forward earnings, the 2nd percentile of ten years. Earnings growth and the 5% dividend yield pay the holder while the 2031 question is decided. A re-rating, which supplies almost all of the model's return, needs the market's worry about 2031 to start clearing. Whether that worry clears depends on what management buys and what it pays, and the first evidence arrives at the strategy update in early December 2026.

The bet in one line. At 8.2 times, a holder earns about 13% to end-2027 if the multiple never moves, about 2% if it falls back to its five-year low, and 35% to 54% if it moves part of the way back to normal: the risk/reward is skewed to the positive by where the multiple starts, not by aggressive forecasts.

What matters most.

  1. The positive skew is in the share price, not in the earnings. On operations, my forecasts sit within 1% to 2% of consensus for 2026 to 2028. Guidance raises are about four times as likely as cuts, but they will be modest and late. The asymmetry comes from the starting multiple: a positive return if the multiple never moves, roughly nothing lost at the five-year-low multiple, and a large gain on even a partial return to a normal multiple (#12).
  2. Restraint cannot clear the 2031 worry; only a good purchase can. A EUR 10bn buyback gives the best per-share arithmetic available, yet it leaves the 2031 question unanswered. A commercial-stage asset bought at a defensible price is the only action that addresses 2031, and it costs earnings first and probably the AA credit rating. The shares fell 2.9% on the report that Sanofi is weighing a purchase of Insmed. The right test of a deal is the asset's stage and price, not its size.
  3. The oral threat to Dupixent became real on 23 November 2026. Kymera's pill KT-621 showed efficacy in the range of the injectable drugs in a Phase 2b trial. The KT-621 result changes no forecast before 2030. It does lower the ceiling on Sanofi's multiple until the long-acting successor antibodies that Sanofi shares with Regeneron show data, and Sanofi ended its own oral programme three weeks before the KT-621 result.
  4. Sanofi's operating leverage is half-shared with Regeneron. Sanofi keeps about 45 cents of operating profit from each extra euro of Dupixent sales. Sales upgrades have reached EPS one for one, the operating margin rises about half a point a year, and price, not cost, is the most powerful operating lever.
  5. 2027 has a known shape. The first quarter (reported in late April) should be comfortable; the second quarter (late July) is the trough, with EPS flat to down; comparisons are clean from the second half. The first proper window for estimate upgrades is October 2027 to early 2028.
  6. Three small favourable gaps are missing from the market's narrative. Management has beaten its first annual EPS guide in seven years out of seven. Gross-to-net releases, which brokers treat as one-off, have recurred and grown for three years. A group of stale low broker estimates must rise when 2026 results are reported.
  7. The stock is turning up, not yet reinforcing. Earnings and guidance have turned; the share price, broker ratings and the discount to peers have not. The guideline fair multiple of 13.59 times was last seen in 2017, so I read the model's return of about 90% as the outcome if the 2031 worry clears, not as the central expectation.

The five judgements that will move the shares most (arithmetic in #9): what management does with the balance sheet; how much of Dupixent's profit survives or is replaced after 2031; Dupixent's volume growth in 2027 and 2028; net price, including the 2028 US contracting round; and the euro-dollar exchange rate.

Where I differ from the market. I agree with the consensus account of Sanofi's business almost everywhere, and the low multiple already reflects the negatives in that account in full. I differ on four points: a large deal should be judged on the asset's stage and price, and could be the event that starts the re-rating; the first 2027 guide, due in January, will look weak on growth but be in line with consensus in euros; gross-to-net releases are a recurring source of upside; and the guideline fair multiple is too high for the stock's present lifecycle phase.

#1 Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Structural demand and capped US pricing make the operating environment strongly supportive through 2027; the dated headwinds all bear on Dupixent, and they gather from 2028.

Evidence: the tailwinds. Demand for Sanofi's growth franchises is structural, not cyclical. Advanced-therapy penetration is about 20% in US atopic dermatitis and in single digits in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), against 40% to 50% in psoriasis, the nearest precedent, where several blockbusters grew together. More than 1.5 million patients take Dupixent, a chronic therapy, so each year's new patients add to the base; Dupixent sales grew 34.8% at constant currency in the third quarter of 2026.

US policy has moved from an open-ended threat to a capped cost. The December 2025 pricing agreement bought Sanofi a tariff exemption to January 2029; Dupixent is outside Medicare price negotiation until about 2031; the November 2026 midterm elections produced divided government; and the 2027 formularies are published with Dupixent's position intact.

Evidence: the headwinds. The headwinds are real, and each has a date. Dupixent's share of new atopic dermatitis patients who have never had a biologic has fallen from 80%-90% to 30%-40%, as Lilly's Ebglyss and Galderma's Nemluvio win new patients with less frequent dosing. On 23 November 2026 Kymera's oral drug KT-621 met every endpoint in its Phase 2b trial, with caveats on dose and eye safety (figure below). KT-621's Phase 3 trial starts by mid-2027, and Morgan Stanley expects KT-621 to erode Dupixent's first-line use by late 2030. AbbVie's long-acting antibody zumilokibart targets a 2029 launch.

Three further headwinds sit outside Dupixent. Vaccines, about 17% of sales, face hostile US policy, competition from Merck's Enflonsia and lower flu immunisation. Germany's mandatory rebate rises from 7% to 15.5% in January 2027. The US dollar is now 60% of Sanofi's sales, against a euro-heavy cost base.

Inference. The environment has a time structure: tailwinds dominate through 2027, and headwinds dominate from 2028. Because Dupixent is a chronic therapy, lost share of new patients reaches revenue slowly, and reaches it first as higher rebates. US net price for 2027 is already largely contracted. The price exposure has moved to the 2028 contracting round, negotiated during 2027, just as the three large pharmacy benefit managers shift to fee-based models that weaken the incumbent's rebate advantage.

So what. The environment underwrites the forecasts to 2028 with high confidence and, at the same time, explains why the market will not pay for them: every adverse force converges on one product in 2029 to 2033.

Strongest counter-case. The bear case is that Dupixent's turn will come faster than the arithmetic of a chronic patient base suggests: the oral drug class is now validated, payers are gaining tools, and Sanofi has no oral drug of its own. The bull case is that competitors' advertising enlarges the treated market, dermatologists say they will not switch stable patients, and Regeneron's chief scientist doubts that pills will beat long-acting antibodies on safety or convenience.

What would change my view. Negatively: US Dupixent prescriptions growing less than about 12% into early 2027; an exclusion or step requirement for Dupixent in a 2028 formulary; a Phase 3 design for KT-621 that includes a head-to-head arm against Dupixent. Positively: Dupixent sales growing faster than 17% in the first quarter of 2027, with COPD as the engine.

Market and me. I agree with the market on both the strength of demand and the dated headwinds. I differ on timing: 2027 US net price is safer than feared, 2028 US net price is less safe, and the KT-621 result is an event for the multiple, not for earnings before 2030.

Conclusion: the tailwinds are strong and visible through 2027; the headwinds are not absent but dated, they converge on Dupixent from 2028, and one of them, a credible oral competitor, became fact this week.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. Structural under-penetration (about 20% in US atopic dermatitis, single digits in COPD) and a chronic, accumulating Dupixent base, with US pricing capped to 2029 and 2027 formularies intact, add strongly to growth through 2027; but share of new patients has fallen to 30-40%, a validated oral (KT-621) and long-acting rivals, hostile vaccine policy (17% of sales), the German rebate rise, the 2028 PBM round and a 60% dollar weight trim it from 2028, and consensus sales growth sits only at the 55th percentile. An offset but clear net positive, just above the External change forces group (57), placed below Linea Directa's advanced cycle and above OEM's modest recovery.

#2 Internally driven corporate change

Sanofi's new management has repaired costs and focus quickly; for the share price over the next year, the internal change that matters is a single capital decision.

Evidence. Almost the whole top team changed in nine months. The board declined to renew the previous chief executive's mandate; Belén Garijo took over on 1 May 2026; Paulo Fontoura became head of R&D on 1 September; and the finance chief, François Roger, added business development to his remit. The new team's first acts were cuts: two late-stage immunology assets were stopped, and every move from Phase 2 to Phase 3 was halted pending review.

Costs are being held: in the third quarter of 2026 R&D rose 0.8% and selling and administrative costs fell 0.9%, on sales up 14%. The portfolio is narrower: the consumer business is deconsolidated, and 20 mature medicines and three plants go to Cheplapharm during 2027. The Regeneron relationship was reset in October 2026: the two companies ended their litigation and added four long-acting antibodies, dosed every three to six months, with registration studies from late 2027 or early 2028.

Against those strengths, failures and cuts have emptied the internal late-stage pipeline, the multiple sclerosis readout for frexalimab has slipped to 2028, and Sanofi terminated its own oral STAT6 degrader on 3 November 2026. Restructuring has been charged in each of the last eight years. Former employees describe a transactional culture after repeated reorganisations. Management now says openly that existing assets cannot cover the post-2031 gap and that it will fund larger, later-stage purchases.

Inference. The changes are broad, fast and well financed, but mostly defensive. They underwrite the 2026 to 2028 earnings path. The one change that would alter the long-term case, a bridge across 2031, has to be bought. Part of the margin improvement is also a change in where the cost of renewing the portfolio is recorded: purchased and licensed assets are capitalised and their amortisation sits outside BOI (business operating income, Sanofi's adjusted operating profit after Regeneron's share of Dupixent profit), whereas internal R&D would have been expensed inside it.

So what. For the share price over the next year, the internal change force that matters is a single decision about capital. Everything else management has changed is already in the numbers.

Strongest counter-case. The bear case is that new management still runs the same research engine. A chief executive whose record at Merck KGaA on late-stage assets and mid-term targets was mixed is about to make the largest purchase in Sanofi's history, in the most crowded asset market the industry has seen, days after a rival's data weakened her negotiating hand. The bull case rests on the AstraZeneca precedent of 2011, which Redburn cites: a post-mortem of research followed by a fivefold rise in late-stage success.

What would change my view. A strategy update that states a return hurdle and a leverage limit, and then keeps them; the stage and price of the first deal; evidence in 2027 that R&D stays flat while registration studies begin.

Market and me. The market credits management for operations (estimates are up) and withholds credit for strategy (the share of buy ratings is falling). I agree, and add one point: the Regeneron reset is under-rated. Long-acting injectables are what the two strongest incumbents, Regeneron and AbbVie, are betting on against the pill, and Sanofi holds half of four of them, with its sales force already in place.

Conclusion: corporate change is strong and credible on execution and cost, absent on organic renewal, and about to be defined by one capital decision.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. A near-complete top-team change in nine months, cost held (R&D +0.8% and SG&A -0.9% on sales +14%), a narrowed perimeter (consumer out, Cheplapharm sale) and the Regeneron reset adding four long-acting antibodies are broad, funded and already underpin the 2026-28 earnings path; but they are mostly repair, the internal pipeline has been emptied, the own oral was dropped, restructuring recurs yearly, and the one move that would change the long-term case, a large purchase, is not yet made. Complete self-help that mainly repairs a mature business sits in the low 60s, coherent with the group (63): above Odfjell's single deal, below OEM's turned engine.

#3 Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Sanofi is a medium-quality, non-cyclical business whose moat is commercial and finite, renewed only by buying, under a management that is capable but untested where it now matters most.

Evidence. The industry structure is supportive for exactly as long as a patent lasts: gross margins near 80%, high regulatory barriers and, in vaccines, a four-company oligopoly. The structure turns hostile at patent expiry, and the buyers are concentrated: three purchasing groups cover about 85% of US claims, and their owners now run private-label biosimilars (one of them moved 97% of its Humira patients to a biosimilar within a season).

Sanofi's advantage is commercial. Dupixent leads its category on breadth (nine indications), safety record and physician familiarity, and about 80% of patients stay on it. Dupixent's composition patent runs to March 2031; management aims to defer biosimilars to 2032 or 2033 with later patents. The advantage Sanofi lacks is research productivity: over ten years it spent about as much on R&D as AstraZeneca, with far poorer output.

The financial profile is mixed. Consensus operating margin is 27% to 28%, against 31% at GSK, 33% to 36% at AstraZeneca and 39% to 40% at Novartis; the gap is Regeneron's share of Dupixent profit, about 15% of group sales, not inefficiency. Return on invested capital is about 10%, against 14% to 16% at the stronger peers. Free cash flow is about 80% to 85% of business net income, and the balance sheet is rated AA. The earnings base is not clean: reported EPS was EUR 4.26 in 2025 against business EPS of EUR 7.83, and counting the recurring restructuring charges as a cost would lower business EPS by about 6%.

Management is decisive and candid, and sets pragmatic rather than stretching goals. Sanofi's capital allocation record has a clear pattern: purchases of commercial-stage assets close to existing franchises worked (Genzyme, Bioverativ and, so far, Blueprint); early-stage purchases did not (Translate Bio, Kiadis, Provention).

Inference. Sanofi's working model is "buy science, sell well". Its moat is a legacy moat being consumed, not a compounding one, and it is renewed only by buying. Sanofi's own deal record supplies the rule for judging the next deal: the asset's stage and its adjacency to existing franchises decide the outcome.

So what. Sanofi is a medium-quality, non-cyclical business with an above-average margin structure and cash generation, below-average returns and earnings quality, and a management whose test lies ahead in renewing the portfolio, historically Sanofi's weakest area.

Strongest counter-case. Quality may be better than it screens: without Regeneron's profit share Sanofi's margin would exceed its peers', the vaccines oligopoly is durable, and the commercial organisation has value beyond 2031 that the market prices at close to nothing (Redburn has put Sanofi's value with no pipeline contribution at about EUR 98 a share). Or quality may be worse than it screens: an adjusted-earnings definition that excludes acquisition amortisation flatters the buy-not-build strategy just as Sanofi adopts that strategy.

What would change my view. A dated settlement or court win on the later Dupixent patents; a first large deal that states and meets a return hurdle; an internally discovered asset succeeding in Phase 3.

Market and me. I agree with the market's reading, which Bernstein's 30% valuation discount to European peers captures. I differ in emphasis: Sanofi's scarce asset is its selling organisation, and that organisation can be transferred to bought products and to the long-acting successors.

Conclusion: the industry structure and the Dupixent franchise are favourable inside the forecast window and finite beyond it, the financial profile is average overall, and management is capable but unproven where it now matters most.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. A high-barrier, non-cyclical industry with an 80% gross margin and a vaccines oligopoly, and a category-leading commercial franchise, but the moat is a legacy one with a 2031 expiry, renewed only by buying, against concentrated PBM buyers, with poor R&D productivity and a mixed early-stage deal record; the figures show top-quartile margins (gross 86th, operating 79th percentile) and AA balance sheet but ROIC about 10% (5.5% reported, 41st) below peers and an adjusted earnings base that excludes recurring restructuring. Average overall, coherent with the four groups (50/46/55/46): just below Shell's well-run commodity franchise, above Xvivo's unproven moat.

#4 Guidance: conservatism and track record

Sanofi's annual guidance is conservative and reliably beaten; its statements beyond one year are neither, and deserve a discount.

Evidence. Sanofi raised its 2026 guidance three times, from high-single-digit sales growth in January to low-teens sales growth and mid-teens business EPS growth on 30 October. The model's 2026 EPS growth is about 16% to 17% at constant currency, at or above the top of the guided range, and the guidance implies a fourth quarter roughly flat on last year even though sales are growing about 10%. In each of the seven years from 2020 to 2026, delivery exceeded the first guide by 2 to 7 points of EPS growth. The first raise has always come with the half-year results, never with the first quarter. The one adverse precedent is October 2023, when management withdrew a margin target in order to spend more.

Management keeps expectations for 2027 low in a specific way: it quantifies every headwind (about EUR 1.3bn of divested sales, the end of Regeneron's development reimbursement, slightly negative price, flat R&D) and only describes every offset. Sanofi has set no margin or EPS target beyond the current year since 2023, and management's statement that Dupixent's patent expiry will have "only a moderate" revenue effect is unquantified and at odds with brokers' models.

Inference. Annual guidance is conservative and reliable; mid-term statements are neither. I expect the first 2027 guide, on 28 January 2027, to be mid-single-digit sales growth with EPS growing in the mid-to-high single digits at constant currency. Applied to a 2026 result near EUR 9.05, EPS growth of 5% to 7% gives EUR 9.50 to EUR 9.68, which brackets the consensus mean (EUR 9.50) and median (EUR 9.70). The guided growth rate will look a point or two short of consensus; the guided level in euros will be in line. The model's forecast without an acquisition (EUR 9.74, +7.6%) assumes the smallest beat in the seven-year record. A typical beat of 4 to 6 points would mean EUR 9.95 to EUR 10.15.

So what. Management's beating habit is the best-founded favourable gap in the case: either management guides lower than I expect, or the forecasts are conservative against management's own habits. A weak share-price reaction to the January headline would be a misreading.

Strongest counter-case. The beating habit may not hold in 2027. The half-year print is the weakest of the year, so the usual July raise is unlikely. The 2026 base may be inflated by a further gross-to-net release that management then guides against. A completed large acquisition would be restated into the guide and produce a lower headline number; I put the chance of such a restatement at about 30% during 2027 or early 2028.

What would change my view. A January guide with EPS growing only in line with sales, or by less than 5%; a fourth quarter showing a large catch-up in costs.

Market and me. Brokers expect conservative framing across the sector, so we agree on direction. None that I have seen spells out the base effect that will make the January guide look weaker than it is, or the later-than-usual timing of the first raise in 2027.

Conclusion: annual guidance is conservative, with a seven-for-seven record of being beaten, which is a real asset to the case; every statement beyond one year deserves a discount.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. The first annual guide has been beaten by 2-7 points of EPS growth in seven years out of seven, 2026 was raised three times and current guidance implies a flat Q4 on sales up about 10%, so it is conservative now; held back because nothing is guided beyond one year, mid-term statements (the withdrawn 2023 margin target, the unquantified 'moderate' 2031 effect) are unreliable, and consensus for 2027 is already full (Sell-side estimates group 45 against Guidance 66). Below Maersk's repeated low-set-and-raise run, above Odfjell's cycle-helped beat.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Sanofi's operating leverage is real but half-shared with Regeneron and partly spent on price, so profit grows only a little faster than sales until 2028; launch medicines and price, not Dupixent volume, are the levers to watch.

Evidence. Sanofi keeps about 45 cents of BOI for each extra euro of Dupixent sales, because Regeneron takes half of US Dupixent profit and 35% to 45% elsewhere. The third quarter of 2026 bears this out: Dupixent sales rose about EUR 1.47bn, and the expense line that carries Regeneron's share rose EUR 0.87bn (part of that rise was the end of Regeneron's development reimbursement). Sanofi keeps about 80 cents of each euro of launch-medicine sales (an estimate; Sanofi does not disclose it) and loses about 55 cents of BOI for each euro of general-medicines sales that goes.

R&D and selling costs together fall from 39.7% of sales in 2025 to about 31.7% in 2030, which is 8 points of fixed-cost leverage. Only about 3.5 of those points reach the BOI margin (from about 27.7% to 31.2%). The rest is absorbed by Regeneron's rising share, the end of the development reimbursement, royalty step-ups to Sobi, and price.

Sanofi has no pricing power: price added about a point to 2026 sales growth only through gross-to-net releases, and it subtracts 1 to 1.3 points a year from 2027. The revision data show the consequence of weak gearing. Over twelve months, consensus 2027 sales rose 5% and consensus 2027 EPS also rose 5%, whereas a business with ordinary gearing would show EPS revisions of 1.3 to 1.5 times its sales revisions.

Financial leverage is low, at about 0.9 times EBITDA, and amplifies nothing. The reinforcing feedback loop is Dupixent's accumulating patient base, which keeps the average number of patients on therapy growing about 17% in 2027 and 10% in 2028 even as Dupixent's share of new patients falls. The balancing loops are Regeneron's profit share and the dollar, whose weight in Sanofi's sales rises with every US sale.

Inference. In 2027, revenue growth leads to proportionate profit growth, not outsized growth (sales +5.0%, EPS +6.6%). The gearing is better in 2028, the first year with clean comparisons (BOI +8.6% on sales +6.0%). Launch medicines are where the leverage sits: they add about EUR 1.0bn to 2027 BOI, against Dupixent's EUR 1.3bn, on a quarter of Dupixent's sales.

So what. Do not expect Dupixent beats to gear earnings. Watch launches and price: a euro of launch sales is worth nearly twice a euro of Dupixent sales, and one point of price is worth more than one point of volume.

Strongest counter-case. Underlying leverage is stronger than the reported figures show. Excluding non-recurring items, disposals and the assumed acquisition, 2027 needs BOI to grow about 17% on sales growth of about 8%, and 2026 delivered the same ratio with the same levers. On this view the underlying gearing is about two times, masked by known items, and it will show from 2028.

What would change my view. Disclosure of launch-medicine margins; R&D resuming growth early as registration studies start; a second year of costs held flat.

Market and me. The terms of the Regeneron contract are universally known. Their consequences are not quantified: I found no broker stating the 45 cents, the one-for-one pass-through of sales upgrades to EPS, or that price outweighs volume.

Conclusion: Sanofi has real operating leverage that is half-shared and partly spent on price, so profit grows a little faster than sales, not much faster, until the comparisons clear in 2028.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. The structure has real fixed-cost leverage (R&D and selling costs fall 8 points of sales by 2030) and a reinforcing patient-base loop, but Sanofi keeps only about 45 cents of each extra Dupixent euro, has no pricing power (price takes 1-1.3 points a year from 2027) and low debt that amplifies nothing, so only 3.5 margin points reach BOI and twelve-month revisions passed sales to EPS one for one; forecast EPS grows about 1.3 times sales against the Universe's typical 2. Launch medicines (about 80 cents kept) are the real gear, which keeps it off the 25 level, but it sits below the ordinary mix, coherent with Economic strength (55) and Financial forecasts (40).

#6 Forecast financials

After a 15% year in 2026, the forecasts show a well-anchored 6% to 8% a year of EPS growth to 2029, better than Sanofi's past and close to consensus; double digits need a buyback or management's usual guidance beat.

The forecasts of record (the model; EUR; net sales basis).

FY2025A FY2026 FY2027 FY2028 FY2029 FY2030
Net sales (bn) 43.6 48.6 51.1 54.1 56.1 57.3
Growth +11.5% +5.0% +6.0% +3.7% +2.1%
EBITDA margin (BOI plus depreciation) about 30.8% 32.3% 32.8% 33.6% 34.3% 34.6%
Business EPS 7.83 9.02 9.61 10.38 11.08 11.43
Growth +15.2% +6.6% +8.0% +6.7% +3.2%
Business EPS with no acquisition (cross-check) 9.74 10.48 10.99 11.23
Consensus EPS, median 9.00 9.70 10.58 11.35

Equity free cash flow (bn) 7.8 8.8 9.6 11.2 11.7

On the business basis, 2026 EPS growth is 15.2%; the 80% shown in the model summary is not comparable (end-note 3).

Evidence and inference. Double-digit EPS growth is a 2026 event. From 2027 to 2029 EPS grows 6% to 8% a year, and 3% in 2030 as Dupixent flattens ahead of its patent expiry. Against the past this is a clear step up: business EPS fell from EUR 8.26 in 2022 to EUR 7.83 in 2025, whereas the forecasts compound at about 8% a year from 2025 to 2030, with the margin rising about half a point a year. The step up in growth is front-loaded: about 2.5 points of 2026's EPS growth come from items that do not recur.

Within 2027, the first half is the trough. The end of Regeneron's reimbursement, the base effects of 2026's one-off gains and the start of the Cheplapharm transfer all land in the first half, giving first-half EPS growth of 3% to 4% and second-half growth of about 8%.

Free cash flow after restructuring is about EUR 7.5bn in 2026 and EUR 8.6bn in 2027, a yield of 7% to 8% on the market value, and it covers the dividend about 1.5 times. On the company's definition, net debt is about EUR 11.7bn at end-2026 and EUR 19.4bn at end-2027, 1.2 times EBITDA. The model's higher net-debt figures use a different, lease-inclusive definition and do not signal a breach of management's leverage guide (end-note 4).

So what. There is scope for higher growth and margins than in the past, and little scope for double-digit growth without help. The two routes to double digits are a buyback and management's habit of beating its guide, and neither is in the forecasts.

Strongest counter-case. The outer years lean on strengths Sanofi has not shown. By 2030 the assumed acquired asset supplies about a fifth of cumulative BOI growth, Dupixent is forecast 6% above the company's own 2030 ambition just as long-acting and oral rivals arrive, and Sanofi's record on mid-term targets is poor. The 2029 consensus rests on only 12 brokers, and I expect it to be trimmed.

What would change my view. Fourth-quarter Dupixent sales well short of about EUR 5.5bn; launch-medicine growth below 20%; R&D guided to grow in 2027.

Market and me. For 2026 to 2028 the forecasts sit between the consensus mean and median, so we agree. For 2029 they are about 2.4% below the median. The material difference is below the operating line: consensus debt falls every year, so consensus contains neither an acquisition nor a buyback, which is the one outcome I judge least likely. I changed no forecast input for this week's news: the KT-621 result and the Insmed report bear on the years after 2030 and on the multiple, not on the inputs.

Conclusion: the forecasts show a well-anchored 6% to 8% a year of EPS growth after a 15% year, better than Sanofi's past and short of double digits unless capital is returned or guidance is beaten by the usual margin.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. 5-10% gives C; placed in the upper-middle of the band because the margin rises about half a point a year above a record of EPS falling from 2022 to 2025 and the growth is largely organic, but held below the top of the band because about 2.5 points of 2026's 15% do not recur, growth slows to 3% by 2030 and the outer years lean partly on an assumed acquisition.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Operating upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months are mildly skewed up, well signposted and late; the capital decision is the larger swing, in either direction.

Evidence: guidance. Over the six earnings events to April 2028, I put the chance of at least one guidance raise in 2027 at about 60% and of an operating cut at about 12%. The likely sequence is: 2026 delivered at or above the top of its range (70%); a first 2027 guide that brackets the consensus mean in euros; no change in April; and a raise in October 2027 (45%) more likely than in July (35%).

Evidence: estimates. Consensus for 2027 is really two groups of brokers: seven between EUR 8.49 and EUR 9.17, and eight between EUR 9.51 and EUR 10.07, with nothing between. The low group looks stale. Five brokers hold 2026 estimates of EUR 8.52 to EUR 8.69, which, with about EUR 7.51 reported for nine months, would require a fourth quarter 20% to 35% below last year's. When 2026 is reported, those five brokers must raise their 2026 estimates by 4% to 6% and will carry part of the increase into 2027. The high group needs 2027 growth of 10% to 12% and is exposed at the half-year. Net, I expect the 2027 consensus mean to end within 2% of today's EUR 9.50 (60%), with higher (25%) more likely than lower (15%).

One source of upside is in no model. Prior-period rebate releases (gross-to-net releases) were EUR 155m in 2023, EUR 282m in 2024 and EUR 667m in 2025, and brokers identified about EUR 0.45bn to 0.5bn in two quarters of 2026. The forecasts assume none in 2027. The annual report in February 2027 is the test of whether the releases recur.

The largest prospective revision is not operational. A completed purchase of EUR 25bn or more (about 35% likely by end-2027) would cut 2028 consensus EPS by 3% to 5% in one step; a buyback of EUR 5bn or more (about 15% likely) would add 4% to 8%.

Evidence: narrative. The sell-side account of Sanofi is complete on the negatives. It can improve only from four sources: the December strategy update, the quality of what Sanofi buys, clinical data on the long-acting antibodies, and the later Dupixent patents.

Inference. Operating upgrades will be modest and back-end loaded: positive breadth into April, risk in July, and positive again from October. This is not a setup in which upgrades are unusually skewed to the positive. It is one in which they are mildly skewed, well signposted, and overshadowed by a step change in either direction from capital deployment.

So what. The 6-to-12-month window contains a small favourable drift in estimates and one large event of uncertain sign. An investor relying on upgrades alone is early; an investor relying on the December event carries that event's risk.

Strongest counter-case. The bull case is Bernstein's: estimates 4% to 11% above consensus for 2026 to 2028, because the growth of the biologics market is underappreciated, which is also what a typical guidance beat would deliver. The bear case is July 2027: first-half EPS growth of 3% to 4% forces the high group of brokers to cut.

What would change my view. A February annual report showing another large release with rebate provisions still rising (more upside); first-quarter Dupixent growth above 17% (an earlier raise); a transaction closing early in 2027 (estimates down sooner).

Market and me. Where the earlier work called 2027 consensus "full", I agree for the median and for July, and disagree for the mean and for the next three months, when the first move in estimates should be up.

Conclusion: there is scope for modest upgrades, more in breadth than in size and later in 2027 than Sanofi's habit, with the acquisition, which is in the narrative but in nobody's numbers, as the swing factor.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is about four times likelier to be raised than cut in the window (about 60% for a raise, more likely October 2027 than July) but the raise will be modest against 5% revenue growth, and the January guide will look short on growth; consensus 2027 is likely flat to slightly up (stale low brokers must lift 2026 by 4-6%, unmodelled gross-to-net releases), offset by a 35% chance of a large deal cutting 2028 consensus 3-5%; the narrative is complete on the negatives and can only improve from the December update. A small, mildly favourable gap, coherent with The fourth set (54): just above Spie's plausible modest raise, below Hexatronic's beat-led momentum.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, share price and peers

Momentum is positive but does not yet confirm the case: strong in guidance, moderate in estimates, absent in conviction, and borrowed from the sector in the share price.

Evidence. Guidance momentum is strong: three raises in 2026. Sell-side momentum is moderate: consensus 2027 EPS is up 4% in one month and 5% in twelve, target prices are up 6% in a month, and the dashboard's sell-side momentum rating is C (19 November 2026). Conviction has not followed: the share of buy ratings is 31%, down 3 points in the same month in which estimates rose.

Price momentum is modest and partly borrowed from the sector. The shares are up 7.0% over three months, 8.6% over six and 2.9% over twelve, at the 60th percentile of relative strength, and 10.5% above a 200-day moving average that has risen in only one of the last twelve months. The dashboard's technical rating is C and its valuation rating A. Over the last six months Sanofi and an equal-weighted basket of European pharma stocks each rose about 13%, with Sanofi's sensitivity to the sector at 1.1, the highest in two years. Roughly 60% of Sanofi's gain came from a higher multiple, matching the sector's re-rating. The clearest move that was Sanofi's own went the other way: the fall on the Insmed report.

Positioning is cautious: short interest is 1.2% of the free float, twice the peer median, and the put-to-call ratio is about two. Morgan Stanley calls the story "catalyst-light".

Key peers are split. Roche (+43% over twelve months) and Novartis (+24%) have strong price momentum. AstraZeneca (-2.5%) rates F on both technical and earnings momentum, and GSK (+3.8%) rates D on both.

Inference. A year of rising estimates went unrewarded: the share price rose less than estimates, so Sanofi's multiple fell slightly while two peers were re-rated.

So what. Momentum does not yet confirm the case. The part of the valuation discount that is specific to Sanofi has not begun to close, and the recent price strength is the reversible, sector-driven kind.

Strongest counter-case. The bull reading is that this is what an early turn looks like: estimates rising, the share price above every moving average, valuation at the floor, and sceptical positioning that can unwind. The bear reading is that Sanofi's nearest comparables in "cheap defensive pharma", GSK and AstraZeneca, have weak momentum, and a rotation out of defensive shares would take Sanofi down by slightly more than its peers.

What would change my view. The share of buy ratings rising with estimates; the 200-day average turning up for several months; Sanofi outperforming on days the sector falls.

Market and me. No difference. The market's "show me" stance is what I would expect from the evidence.

Conclusion: momentum is positive but not strong: C ratings on estimates and technicals, a sector-driven price recovery, and a narrative that is waiting for the capital decision.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Both measures positive and none strongly negative gives B; placed at the floor because guidance momentum is strong (three raises in 2026) and 2027 EPS is up 4% in a month, but revisions over three and six months are only 1% (55th/50th percentile), the share of Buy ratings fell to 31-33% (27th percentile), the 200-day average has risen in one month of twelve, the price gain is sector-borrowed and the nearest peers (AstraZeneca, GSK) are weak.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and the case

The forecasts are simple and low-risk; the investment case is not. Four variables explain the next 18 months of earnings (Dupixent volume and price, the dollar, and capital deployment), and the main one, Dupixent, is the best-observed product in the company: US prescriptions are reported weekly, and Regeneron reports the same sales in dollars on the same day. The plausible range for 2027 EPS is about EUR 9.0 to EUR 10.3 around the model's EUR 9.61. Operations alone account for about 4% either side; currency and corporate action supply the rest. Consensus EPS has in fact moved by about that much in each recent year. The case is harder to judge than the forecasts, because its value depends on an acquisition of unknown size, price and quality, and on a debate about 2031 that 18 months of delivery will not settle.

The five judgements, and what each is worth if wrong.

  1. What management does with the balance sheet. The base case is a EUR 10bn debt-funded purchase in mid-2027, giving 2028 EPS of EUR 10.38.

    • If instead Sanofi makes an Insmed-scale purchase at about EUR 31bn (Jefferies' estimate at a 30% premium): extra debt of EUR 21bn at 3.3% is EUR 0.69bn of interest; after tax at 20.5%, EUR 0.55bn; over 1,203m shares, EUR 0.46. If the asset earns no more in 2028 than the base case's assumed asset, 2028 EPS is about EUR 9.92, 4.4% lower. Each further EUR 0.1bn of operating profit from the asset gives back about EUR 0.07. Net debt would be about EUR 40bn at end-2027, about 2.4 times EBITDA, against management's guide of about 1 time.
    • If instead Sanofi buys back EUR 10bn of shares at EUR 84: 119m shares are retired (9.9%). Net income with no purchase is EUR 12.61bn (EUR 10.48 times 1,203m shares); less after-tax interest of EUR 0.26bn, EUR 12.35bn; over 1,084m shares, EUR 11.39, 9.7% above the model.
    • The two outcomes are EUR 1.47 apart, 14% of 2028 EPS, which is wider than every operating uncertainty combined. Business EPS excludes the amortisation of what Sanofi buys, so the cut to estimates after a purchase will understate the purchase's economic cost; the share price will move first.

  2. How much of Dupixent's profit survives or is replaced after 2031. This judgement drives the multiple, not near-term EPS. Brokers model about EUR 20bn of Dupixent sales lost within three years of patent expiry. At 45 cents kept per euro, that loss is EUR 9bn of BOI, about half of the EUR 17.9bn forecast for 2030; after tax and over 1,203m shares, it is about EUR 5.9 of the EUR 11.43 of 2030 EPS. If the loss is EUR 12bn instead (biosimilars deferred to 2032 or 2033, and part of the patient base moved to the long-acting successors), it is EUR 5.4bn of BOI and EUR 3.6 a share. Each EUR 1bn of Dupixent sales kept is worth about EUR 0.30 of EPS; each EUR 1bn of wholly owned replacement sales, if Sanofi keeps 80 cents as on its launches, is worth about EUR 0.53. The half-share cuts both ways: Sanofi loses only 45 cents of each Dupixent euro lost. Management's own claim, as Deutsche Bank reports it, is that EUR 10bn of new revenue, or EUR 8bn of BOI, would offset the profit effect of the patent expiry.

  3. Dupixent's volume growth in 2027. The base case is +14%. If growth is +9%: 5 points on EUR 20.9bn is EUR 1.05bn of sales (2% of group sales); at 45 cents, EUR 0.47bn of BOI; after tax, EUR 0.37bn; over 1,202m shares, EUR 0.31, or 3.2% of 2027 EPS. The shortfall carries into the 2028 base. Redburn regards Dupixent growth below 10% as the sign of severe competitive problems, so the multiple would react as well.

  4. Net price. The base case is about -1.2 points a year. One further point is 1% of EUR 51.1bn, or EUR 0.51bn of sales; Sanofi keeps about 65% after Regeneron's share, EUR 0.33bn of BOI; after tax, EUR 0.26bn; EUR 0.22 a share, or 2.3%. That one point of price equals 0.65 point of margin, twice the whole margin gain planned for 2027. The mirror image is upside: recurring gross-to-net releases of EUR 0.2bn to 0.4bn would add EUR 0.09 to EUR 0.17 a share. For 2027 the range is narrow because formularies are set; the exposure is in 2028.

  5. The dollar. The base case is EUR/USD 1.16. The company's stated sensitivity is EUR 1,069m of sales and EUR 0.23 of EPS per 0.05 move in the rate. At 1.25, 1.8 times EUR 0.23 is EUR 0.41 lower (4.3%), with sales about EUR 1.9bn lower. At 1.10, EPS is EUR 0.28 higher (2.9%). Hedges on EUR 13.4bn of dollar sales expire during 2027, so 2027 is partly protected and 2028 is not.

Second-order items: five points of launch-medicine growth is worth about EUR 0.14 a share, and one point of unplanned growth in R&D and selling costs about EUR 0.12.

Sudden risks. Three risks are sudden and can be tracked only at the moment of announcement: a transaction; a gross-to-net adjustment (EUR 100m to 300m a quarter, either way); and a share placement by L'Oréal, which holds 7.27% of Sanofi with no lock-up. Two risks are low-probability and very large: a Dupixent safety signal, and a supply interruption (Regeneron manufactures Dupixent; AstraZeneca manufactures Beyfortus and is in arbitration with Sanofi).

Sector and cyclical risk, and precedent. Demand is non-cyclical, but the share is not immune to the sector: peers explain about 38% of its daily variance over six months, and explained 60% during the US tariff and pricing shock of April 2025. Sanofi's own history shows how sudden company-specific falls can be: on month-end prices the shares lost about 15% in August 2022, and again in October 2023, when management withdrew its margin target. Sector precedent says that stocks facing a dominant product's expiry trade on 7 to 10 times earnings, that their multiples typically trough six to seven years before the expiry, and that debt-funded purchases can make matters worse before they help (a credit downgrade at Bristol Myers Squibb; Novartis writing down part of a USD 12bn purchase within seven months).

How far down. A return to the five-year low multiple of 7.3 times on consensus 2027 EPS gives a share price of about EUR 71, 15% below today's; with EPS also cut 5%, about EUR 67, 20% below. The dividend offsets a quarter to a third of that fall over a year.

Strongest counter-case. I may understate the risk: Dupixent's concentration rises inside the forecast window, to 47% of sales in 2027, and the risks are correlated because growth, price, policy and currency all sit in the US. Or I may overstate it: the negatives are known by date, and the multiple already assumes them.

What would change my view. A deal announced with a price and structure would remove the largest unknown, for better or worse. A disclosed gross-to-net reconciliation would make the least observable driver trackable.

Market and me. The market treats Sanofi as a risky case with safe numbers, and so do I.

Conclusion: forecast risk is low and unusually trackable; case risk is moderate and concentrated in one management decision and one product; and the floor multiple limits plausible downside to about 15% to 20%.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The forecasts are simple and trackable: four drivers, the main one observed weekly, a 2027 EPS cone of about -6% to +7% with operations only about 4% either way, non-cyclical demand and debt about 0.9 times EBITDA; but the case carries a sudden capital event within months (an Insmed-scale deal would take 2028 EPS down 4% and leverage to 2.4 times, a buyback up 10%), one product at 43-47% of sales with correlated US price, policy and currency exposure, and a 2031 debate that delivery will not settle, with 15-20% downside to the floor multiple. Between the two Risks groups (55 and 68): below OEM's narrow decentralised range, just above Banca Generali's rate sensitivity.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The stock is turning up, not reinforcing: earnings and estimates have turned, valuation and narrative have not, and the next phase will be decided by events that begin in early December 2026.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places Sanofi in the Reinforcing phase. The fundamentals fit that phase: guidance raised three times, estimates rising, and cost delivery ahead of plan. The stock does not fit it: a 2.9% gain in twelve months in which estimates rose 5% and two peers gained 24% and 43%; a 200-day average that rose in one month of twelve; a falling share of buy ratings; a multiple at the 2nd percentile of ten years, having touched its low of 7.5 times in September 2026; and a recent recovery that tracked the sector.

Inference. I place the stock at turning up: turned in earnings and estimates, not yet in valuation or narrative. Moving on to the broadening phase would require new buyers attracted by a reason beyond cheapness, which for Sanofi means the 2031 worry starting to clear. The 2031 worry has not started to clear, and this week's KT-621 result moved that clearing slightly further away. The stock stands at a fork with a date on it.

So what. A turning-up stock deserves a lower point in its historical multiple range than a reinforcing one, because the forecasts that matter most to its value, those beyond 2030, are still uncertain. This lifecycle placement is the basis for my view of the fair multiple in #11.

Strongest counter-case. The dashboard may be right and I too cautious: three guidance raises and rising estimates are what reinforcing means, and price follows fundamentals with a lag. Against that, a year of delivery has already passed without the price following.

What would change my view. Outperformance on company news, not on sector moves; a re-rating that survives a sector reversal.

Market and me. The market's behaviour, marking estimates up without recommending the shares more strongly, is consistent with the turning-up phase.

Conclusion: the stock is turning up, with reinforcing fundamentals and a valuation still waiting, and the next phase will be decided by events that begin in early December 2026.

Score: 59, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's turning up over the dashboard's Reinforcing and the computed Bottoming: earnings and guidance have turned (three raises, estimates up 5%), but the price rose only 2.9% in twelve months, the 200-day average is flat, Buy ratings are falling and the multiple is at the 2nd percentile, and the event that would broaden the thesis (the 2031 worry clearing) is a fork of uncertain sign that KT-621 pushed slightly further away. Early turning with the cause for concern not yet clearing sits just below Nexans' paused Reinforcing and above Greggs' early turn on falling volumes.

#11 The fair multiple

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple is 13.59 times two-year-forward earnings, the 90th percentile of the stock's ten-year history and the level for the Reinforcing phase. It is 62% to 66% above today's multiple, depending on whether today's multiple is read as 8.4 times (the Phases page, 23 November) or 8.2 times (the model, 20 November). Topic #12 uses the guideline.

My view: 13.59 times is the right multiple for a later phase, and a ceiling for this one; I regard 9.9 to 11.3 times as fair over 18 months. Four reasons support a lower multiple.

  • Phase. If the stock is turning up and not reinforcing (#10), the guideline's own logic points lower in the range.
  • The history behind the percentile. On month-end data the multiple was at or above 13.59 times only in four months of 2017, when Sanofi was a diversified group with a consumer business and no dated patent cliff inside the market's discounting window. The multiple has not exceeded 11.4 times since it stepped down in August 2022, and its five-year high on weekly data is 12.85 times. The 90th percentile describes a company that no longer exists.
  • Precedent. Stocks facing a dominant product's expiry have traded on 7 to 10 times earnings. The re-ratings on record followed visible successors (AbbVie rose from single digits to 17 times once Skyrizi and Rinvoq had scaled) or clinical proof (Deutsche Bank lifted the multiple it applies to Roche to 22 times on late-stage data). Large purchases stabilised earnings without a quick re-rating (AbbVie stayed near 14 times after buying Allergan).
  • This week. A validated oral competitor, with no oral drug of Sanofi's own, makes the debate about Sanofi's value beyond 2031 slightly harder to win in the next 18 months.

What I would regard as fair. About 9.9 times, the five-year median, is a reasonable normal for Sanofi with its patent cliff acknowledged and its capital plan trusted. About 11.3 times, the ten-year median, is reachable if a bridge across 2031 becomes visible: a commercial-stage asset bought at a defensible price, registration-stage data on the long-acting antibodies, or dated protection from the later Dupixent patents. The guideline's 13.59 times needs the market to value Sanofi as if the cliff were solved. The AbbVie precedent shows that this can happen, but AbbVie's re-rating followed scaled successors, which for Sanofi is a 2028-to-2030 event at the earliest. Brokers' own framing is consistent with my range: their targets average about EUR 97, roughly 10 times 2027 earnings, and Jefferies' upside scenario of EUR 120 already assumes the full peer multiple of 14 times.

So what. The case does not need the guideline multiple to work. A partial return to a normal multiple produces a large return (#12), and that partial return is the more useful anchor.

Strongest counter-case. A stock at the 2nd percentile of ten years, with rising estimates, an AA balance sheet and new management, has room for a violent re-rating if one large uncertainty is removed, and Berenberg argues that a successful purchase could by itself restore a double-digit multiple.

What would change my view. Upward: a priced, commercial-stage deal with the credit-rating outcome known, followed by a quarter in which Sanofi re-rates against peers. Downward: an early-stage or contested purchase at a premium above 40%.

Market and me. The market's implied fair multiple is about 10 times. Mine is 9.9 to 11.3 times. The guideline is well above both.

Conclusion: the guideline multiple of 13.59 times is a ceiling that requires the 2031 worry to be resolved; for a stock that is turning up I regard 9.9 to 11.3 times as the plausible fair range over 18 months.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Cheap on both gives A; placed at the floor because part of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year history was built by a diversified group with no dated cliff in the market's window, the turning-up phase and a validated oral rival argue for a lower point in the range, and the memo's own fair multiple is 9.9-11.3 times rather than the 13.59 guideline; but 8.2 times still sits below the five-year median and near the five-year low, so the business warrants more than the market pays.

#12 Total shareholder return

The dependable part of the return, earnings growth plus dividends, is about 13% to end-2027 and 29% to mid-2029; nine-tenths of the model's headline return of about 90% is re-rating.

The return of record (the model, at the guideline fair multiple, from EUR 83.79).

Horizon Total return Annualised Value per share From earnings From the multiple From dividends
To 31 December 2027 +90.2% +79.3% EUR 159.41 +8.2% +66.1% +10.6%
To 30 June 2029 +103.5% +31.4% EUR 170.48 +12.7% +66.1% +16.3%

The earnings and multiple parts multiply; dividends add. The horizons are the model's fixed columns, about 13 and 31 months from today, not 18 and 36.

What drives the return.

  • The multiple is almost the whole return. The move from 8.2 to 13.59 times is 66 points by itself, and the model assumes it is complete by end-2027 and then held. The model's return is therefore a statement about the multiple (#11), not about the business.
  • Earnings add 8% to end-2027 and 13% to mid-2029. This is the growth in two-year-forward EPS: to EUR 11.08, the 2029 forecast, by end-2027. It is the well-founded part of the return, resting on Dupixent volume, launches and held costs, all demonstrated (#6). Because the multiple applies to earnings two years ahead, the return to end-2027 depends on the 2029 forecast, which is less certain than the 2027 forecast.
  • Dividends add about 5% a year. One caution, already raised with the Financial Analyst and not yet answered: the model credits two dividends (EUR 4.33 and EUR 4.55) by 31 December 2027, but Sanofi pays annually in May, so a holder from today receives one. On that reading the dividend part is 5.2% and the total return about 85%. The return to mid-2029 is unaffected.
  • Other cash returns are nil. Routine buybacks only offset employee share issuance. A large buyback would be upside to this line, and the model does not contain one.

The same arithmetic at other multiples (my calculation, using the model's earnings and one dividend to end-2027; three dividends to mid-2029).

Inference. This table is the investment case. Predictable earnings and the dividend return about 13% over 13 months with no re-rating, and roughly nothing is lost if the multiple goes back to its five-year low. Each step back towards a normal multiple adds 20 points or more. The distribution of outcomes is skewed to the positive because of where the multiple starts, not because the forecasts are aggressive.

Strongest counter-case. The downside row is too kind if earnings and the multiple fall together: an expensive purchase that cut two-year-forward EPS by 5% and held the multiple at its five-year low would give a loss of about 8% before the dividend. The upside rows are too kind if a rotation out of defensive shares arrives first.

What would change my view. The size and sign of the change in the multiple after the December update and the first transaction; a change to the 2029 EPS forecast, since each 1% change in that forecast moves the end-2027 return by 1 to 2 points.

Market and me. Brokers' average target, about EUR 97, implies +16% before dividends and corresponds to about 10 times 2027 earnings: the same multiple as my five-year-median row, applied to nearer earnings. The model's return is far above the brokers' because it uses the guideline multiple.

Conclusion: the model's return of about 90% to end-2027 and 104% to mid-2029 is nine-tenths re-rating; the dependable part, earnings growth plus dividends, is worth about 13% and 29% over the same periods, which is what makes the asymmetry attractive.

Score: 82, set by the Rater. About +30% gives B and maps to about 85; I place it at 82 because almost all of the upside is re-rating that depends on the December update and the first deal, and the lower tail (an expensive purchase with the multiple held at its low, about -8% before the dividend) is moderate; the three-year check is supportive (+29% with no re-rating, +52% at 9.9 times to mid-2029), and earnings plus dividend alone give about 13%.

#13 Summary conclusion

Sanofi is a medium-quality, non-cyclical business on a floor multiple, with one large and dated cause for concern: March 2031. The earnings and the dividend pay about 13% over 13 months if nothing changes; a return towards a normal multiple adds roughly 20 to 40 points more; and the plausible downside is limited to about 15% to 20%.

Sanofi's next 18 months are among the most predictable in large-cap European pharma: a chronic, accumulating patient base, held costs, a conservative management that has beaten its first guide seven years running, and a 2027 whose weak second quarter is known in advance. None of that predictability has moved the shares, because the market is pricing March 2031 and the purchase that management has signalled.

The constructive reading is that the share price is set up well for an investor who can wait for the fork. The plausible downside of about 15% to 20% has a known trigger: an expensive or early-stage purchase. The upside, a return towards a normal multiple worth 35% to 55%, also has a known trigger: evidence that the bridge across 2031 is being built at a sensible price. The same event, Sanofi's first large purchase, can supply either outcome. The December strategy update, the first transaction, the January guide and the February annual report will show which, in that order, within three months.

What I would hold on to:

  1. judge the deal by the asset's stage and price, not its size;
  2. do not read the January guide's growth rate as a miss;
  3. do not extrapolate the April 2027 print, or be alarmed by the July 2027 print;
  4. and treat the 13.59 times multiple as what success looks like, not as the base case.

The four memo ratings.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 58, set by the Rater. Input forces are clearly but modestly positive (external 60, internal 62: structural demand and funded self-help, offset by dated price, competition and dollar headwinds and an unmade capital decision), and they reach profits surely in 2026 but then lift EPS only 6-8% a year, below the Universe median (consensus EPS growth 32nd percentile), so the net change sits in the high 50s, a mild net positive.

Foundations' Robustness: 60, set by the Rater. Non-discretionary demand, high regulatory barriers, a vaccines oligopoly, strong cash conversion, an AA balance sheet and a seven-for-seven record of beating annual guidance (topic 4 at 72) make the business more stable than its average quality (topic 3 at 52) alone suggests; but a moat that expires in 2031 with half of profit in one product, no pricing power, weak research productivity and ROIC near 10% keep it from the 75 band.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 60, set by the Rater. The case fits 'Major CfC Clearing in MQ non-cyclical or better business on Q1 multiple' in kind: medium-quality, non-cyclical, a floor multiple and a large, well-defined cause for concern; but the clearing mechanism, the setup's essential element, is not evidenced in the business, cannot come from restraint alone and depends on a purchase of unknown stage and price, while the new oral rival adds to the concern, so one important element is missing.

Case Riskiness: 63, set by the Rater. Topic 9 at 61 is lifted slightly because, as in Richard's CVS reasoning, the operating risks are close to paper cuts (a narrow, trackable cone, conservative guidance) and the multiple is at the bottom of its range, limiting the fall to about 15-20%; but the main risk is not a paper cut: a sudden, near-term capital decision of uncertain quality and a single product at nearly half of sales with an open terminal-value debate keep it well below 75.

End-notes

  1. Terms used throughout. "Business EPS" is Sanofi's adjusted earnings per share, the figure consensus tracks. "BOI" is business operating income, Sanofi's adjusted operating profit after Regeneron's share of Dupixent profit. "Gross-to-net releases" are reversals of rebate accruals made in earlier periods, which add to reported sales. "COPD" is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. "PBM" is a pharmacy benefit manager; "CfC" is cause for concern; "MQ" is medium-quality. Probabilities are my judgements.
  2. Limits of the evidence. The strategy update due in early December 2026 has not happened. The reported approach to Insmed is unconfirmed. The KT-621 trial result is topline only. I have no direct evidence of what investors, as distinct from brokers, are saying; what I say about investors is inferred from the share price, broker ratings and positioning.
  3. 2026 EPS growth in the model summary. The model summary shows 2026 EPS growth of 80%. That figure compares a history line on a different (reported) definition with business EPS and should be ignored. On the business basis, 2026 EPS growth is 15.2%.
  4. Net debt definitions. The model's own net-debt figures (EUR 19.1bn at end-2026 and EUR 26.9bn at end-2027) are on FactSet's lease-inclusive definition and carry an unreconciled difference from the reported periods. They should not be read as a breach of management's leverage guide. On the company's definition, net debt is about EUR 11.7bn and EUR 19.4bn, 1.2 times EBITDA at end-2027.
  5. A check of the multiple's percentile bands. On the 120 month-end values in the valuation history given to me, the multiple was at or above 13.59 times in 4 months, which puts 13.59 times near the 97th percentile of that series, not the 90th. The 90th percentile of that series is about 12.9 times and the 10th about 9.0 times, against the 13.6 and 9.4 stated; the median matches at 11.3. The dashboard may use a finer or differently dated series (the financials block describes the bands as "written at creation"). I have used the guideline as given, and the difference would not change my view.

Appendix: a comment from the Financial Analyst on reporting basis

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.
